router.heading: Read an instruction card.
router.text:
SUNHEARTH 5-CUP RICE COOKER
Quick Start Card

1. Measure the rice with the cup provided. Rinse it under cold water until the water runs clear.
2. Put the rice in the inner pot. Add water up to the line that matches the number of cups (line 2 for two cups).
3. Dry the outside of the pot, place it in the cooker, and close the lid until it clicks.
4. Press COOK. The orange light turns on.
5. When the rice is ready, the cooker switches to KEEP WARM and the green light turns on. Wait ten minutes before opening the lid.

Important:
- Never use metal spoons. They scratch the pot.
- Do not leave rice on KEEP WARM for more than twelve hours.
- Unplug the cooker before cleaning it.

questions.q: According to the card, how much water should be added to the pot?
options: Enough to reach the matching line
Two cups of water for every cup of rice
Enough to make the water run clear
One full measuring cup for each person
questions.why: Step 2: 'Add water up to the line that matches the number of cups.' Clear water (step 1) is about rinsing the rice.

questions.q: What should users do when the green light turns on?
options: Press the COOK button again
Unplug the cooker immediately
Leave the lid closed for a while
Add water up to the next line
questions.why: Step 5: when the green light turns on, 'wait ten minutes before opening the lid'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an instruction on the card?
options: Washing the rice before cooking it
Stirring the rice while it cooks
Drying the outside of the pot
Unplugging the cooker before cleaning it
questions.why: Rinsing (step 1), drying the pot (step 3) and unplugging (last line) are all on the card. Stirring is not.

router.subject: Linguistics
router.title: Two Languages in One Mind
paragraphs: For a long time, many people assumed that bilingual speakers kept their two languages in separate mental boxes and simply opened one at a time. Recent research has shown that this picture is wrong. When bilinguals hear or read a word in one language, related words in their other language become active as well, even if that language is not being used.

This means that a bilingual brain is constantly managing competition. To speak in one language, it must select the right words and hold back those from the other. Some researchers believe that this daily practice strengthens general mental skills, such as focusing attention and switching between tasks. In several experiments, bilingual children and adults performed slightly better than monolinguals on tasks that required ignoring distracting information.

The evidence is not conclusive, however. Other studies, including some with very large groups of participants, have found no such advantage, and the debate continues. Managing two languages also has small costs. Bilinguals usually know fewer words in each language than people who speak only that language, and they more often feel that a word is "on the tip of the tongue." Most researchers agree that these costs are minor compared with the benefit of being able to communicate in two languages.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happens when bilinguals read a word in one of their languages?
options: They translate it silently into the other language.
They need more time than monolinguals to recognize it.
Connected words in their other language are activated too.
Their other language is switched off until it is needed.
questions.why: Paragraph 1: 'related words in their other language become active as well, even if that language is not being used'.

questions.q: The word "conclusive" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: decisive
available
positive
original
questions.why: Conclusive evidence settles a question. The evidence here does not, because 'the debate continues'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a possible effect of using two languages?
options: Being better at ignoring distractions
Knowing fewer words in each language
Failing to recall a familiar word more often
Reading more slowly in both languages
questions.why: Paragraph 2 mentions ignoring distracting information; paragraph 3 mentions fewer words and the tip-of-the-tongue feeling. Reading speed is not discussed.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the studies with very large groups of participants?
options: They were carried out only with bilingual children.
They weaken the claim that bilingualism improves thinking skills.
They showed that bilinguals know more words than monolinguals do.
They proved that the two languages are stored separately.
questions.why: These studies 'found no such advantage', which is why the evidence for stronger mental skills is 'not conclusive'.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the feeling that a word is "on the tip of the tongue"?
options: To show that bilinguals forget their first language over time
To explain how the brain selects words in the right language
To argue that learning a second language is not worth the effort
To illustrate a small disadvantage of managing two languages
questions.why: The sentence follows 'Managing two languages also has small costs' and gives two examples of those costs.

upper.subject: Engineering
upper.title: Learning from Nature's Designs
paragraphs: Engineers facing a difficult problem sometimes look for an answer in an unexpected place: the natural world. This approach is known as biomimicry. Over millions of years, evolution has tested countless designs, and those that survive tend to be efficient. Rather than starting from nothing, a designer can study how a plant or animal has already solved a similar problem.

The best-known example is Velcro. In the 1940s, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed that seeds stuck to his dog's fur after a walk. Under a microscope, he saw that each seed was covered with tiny hooks, and he copied the idea to create a new fastener. Decades later, engineers in Japan reshaped the nose of a high-speed train to resemble the beak of a kingfisher, a bird that dives into water with barely a splash. The redesigned train was quieter when it left tunnels and consumed less electricity.

Biomimicry is not a shortcut, however. Nature builds with materials and methods that factories cannot easily reproduce; spider silk, for instance, is remarkably strong for its weight, yet producing it in large quantities has proved difficult. Moreover, living things are shaped by the need to survive and reproduce, not to serve human purposes, so a natural design usually has to be adapted rather than simply copied.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The history of a popular type of fastener
Why natural materials are stronger than artificial ones
How evolution produces new species of plants and animals
The promise and limits of copying nature in engineering
questions.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 present biomimicry and two successes; paragraph 3 begins 'Biomimicry is not a shortcut, however' and gives its limits.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did George de Mestral see through the microscope?
options: Small hooks on the surface of each seed
A sticky liquid that coated each seed
Fine hairs that tied the seeds together
Sharp points that cut into the fur
questions.why: Paragraph 2: 'he saw that each seed was covered with tiny hooks'.

questions.q: The word "resemble" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: protect
replace
look like
move past
questions.why: To resemble something is to look like it; the train's nose was given the shape of the bird's beak.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the high-speed train before its nose was reshaped?
options: It could not travel through tunnels.
It was noisy when it came out of tunnels.
It needed far less electricity than it does now.
Its nose had been modeled on a different bird.
questions.why: 'The redesigned train was quieter when it left tunnels', so the earlier design was louder at that moment.

questions.q: Why does the author mention spider silk?
options: To give another example of a successful product based on nature
To show that some natural materials are hard to manufacture
To compare the strength of silk with that of steel
To argue that factories should stop using artificial materials
questions.why: It illustrates 'materials and methods that factories cannot easily reproduce': producing silk 'in large quantities has proved difficult'.

router.setting: Listen to an announcement in a classroom.
router.script: Before you go, a word about Thursday's quiz. Several of you have told me that there are too many formulas to memorize in chapter six, and, well, I agree. So I've decided to make the quiz open-book. You may use your textbook and your own handwritten notes, but no phones or laptops. Don't relax too much, though. An open-book quiz means I can ask harder questions, and you'll have only twenty minutes, so you won't have time to look everything up. Know where things are in the chapter before you come.

questions.q: What is the professor mainly doing?
options: Announcing a change in the rules for a quiz
Explaining the formulas in chapter six
Telling students that a quiz has been postponed
Reminding students to buy the textbook
questions.why: 'I've decided to make the quiz open-book', followed by what students may and may not use.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the open-book quiz?
options: It will be shorter than earlier quizzes.
It will cover more chapters than planned.
Students will still need to prepare for it.
Students may share their notes during it.
questions.why: 'Don't relax too much ... you won't have time to look everything up. Know where things are in the chapter before you come.'

router.subject: History
router.script: Today's story starts with a vegetable. I want to argue that the potato, yes, the ordinary potato, changed the history of Europe. Potatoes come from the Andes mountains of South America, where people had grown them for thousands of years. Spanish ships carried them to Europe in the fifteen hundreds. And at first? Almost nobody wanted them. They looked strange, they grew underground, and they belong to the same plant family as some poisonous species, so people didn't trust them. For a long time, in many places, potatoes were mostly fed to animals. So what changed people's minds? Hunger, mainly. A field of potatoes can feed far more people than the same field planted with wheat. Potatoes also grow in poor soil and in cool, wet weather, which describes a lot of northern Europe. And here's a detail I like. In wartime, soldiers could easily carry off the grain stored in a farmer's barn, but potatoes left in the ground were much harder to take. By the seventeen hundreds, rulers such as Frederick the Great of Prussia were actually ordering farmers to plant them. The result was a better-fed population that grew quickly, and many historians think that this growth supplied the workers for Europe's new factories and cities. Not bad for a vegetable nobody wanted.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How farming began in the Andes mountains
Why wheat was replaced by other crops in South America
How a new food crop affected European society
How European armies were fed in wartime
questions.why: The professor wants 'to argue that the potato ... changed the history of Europe' and ends with its effect on population, factories and cities.

questions.q: According to the professor, why did many Europeans refuse to eat potatoes at first?
options: The plant seemed odd and possibly dangerous.
Potatoes cost more than bread.
Rulers did not allow farmers to grow them.
Potatoes spoiled on the long sea journey.
questions.why: 'They looked strange, they grew underground, and they belong to the same plant family as some poisonous species, so people didn't trust them.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention soldiers?
options: To explain how potatoes first reached northern Europe
To show that armies preferred bread to potatoes
To describe who worked in the new factories
To give one advantage of a crop that grows underground
questions.why: Soldiers could carry off stored grain, 'but potatoes left in the ground were much harder to take'.

questions.q: What do many historians believe about Europe's population growth?
options: It caused food shortages in the cities.
It provided labor for growing industries.
It began before potatoes arrived.
It was slower in northern Europe.
questions.why: 'Many historians think that this growth supplied the workers for Europe's new factories and cities.'

router.subject: Chemistry
router.script: Let's start with something you've all seen: ice cubes floating in a glass of water. It looks completely ordinary, right? But it's actually strange. With almost every other substance, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks. Drop a piece of solid wax into melted wax, and down it goes. So why is water different? It comes down to the shape of the water molecule and the way these molecules attract one another. In liquid water, the molecules are constantly moving, sliding past each other, and they can crowd fairly close together. But when water freezes, each molecule locks onto its neighbors in a fixed, open pattern, a bit like people holding hands at arm's length. That pattern has a lot of empty space in it. So the same amount of water takes up about nine percent more room as ice, which makes ice less dense than the water around it. Now, why should you care? Well, think about a lake in winter. Because ice floats, the lake freezes from the top down, and that layer of ice works like a blanket. The water underneath stays liquid, and fish survive until spring. If ice sank, lakes could freeze solid from the bottom up. Life in cold regions would look very different.

questions.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: How fish find food under the ice in winter
Why wax melts at a higher temperature than ice
How lakes in cold regions are formed
Why frozen water is less dense than liquid water
questions.why: The professor asks why ice floats and explains it by the open pattern of molecules in ice, then shows why it matters.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention wax?
options: To describe a substance that never freezes
To show how most substances behave when they are solid
To explain what water molecules are made of
To give an example of a solid that floats
questions.why: Wax illustrates the normal case: 'the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks'. Solid wax goes down, so D is the opposite.

questions.q: According to the professor, what happens to water molecules when water freezes?
options: They join in a fixed pattern with space between them.
They move faster and slide past each other.
They crowd more closely together than before.
They break apart into smaller pieces.
questions.why: 'Each molecule locks onto its neighbors in a fixed, open pattern ... That pattern has a lot of empty space in it.'

questions.q: What does the professor imply would happen if ice were denser than liquid water?
options: Lakes would never freeze at all.
Ice cubes would melt more quickly in a glass.
Fish in cold lakes might not survive the winter.
Lakes would freeze only on the surface.
questions.why: Fish survive because floating ice keeps the water below liquid. 'If ice sank, lakes could freeze solid from the bottom up.'

upper.setting: Listen to a conversation between a student and her thesis supervisor.
script: Professor Aldous, do you have a minute? I've been having second thoughts about my thesis topic.
Oh? You're four months in, Kirra. What's brought this on?
I came across some letters in the city archive, written by dock workers in the nineteen twenties. Nobody's studied them. I'd love to build my thesis around them instead of the newspaper coverage.
It sounds tempting, I'll grant you. But new material has a way of looking better from a distance. Have you actually read them all?
Then here's my suggestion. Finish reading them, and write me two pages on what they'd let you argue that the newspapers don't. If you can't fill two pages, you have your answer.
That's fair. I'll have it to you by the end of the month.

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward the student's new idea?
options: He is enthusiastic and wants her to switch immediately.
He is cautious and wants more evidence before agreeing.
He is annoyed that she visited the archive without asking.
He is certain that the letters are not genuine.
questions.why: 'It sounds tempting, I'll grant you. But new material has a way of looking better from a distance.' He then asks for two pages before deciding.

questions.q: What does the professor mean when he says, "If you can't fill two pages, you have your answer"?
options: A two-page thesis would be too short to be accepted.
He will give his own answer after reading two pages.
Failing to write it would show the new topic is too thin.
The archive holds only two pages of useful letters.
questions.why: The two pages must show what the letters 'let you argue that the newspapers don't'. If she cannot write them, the letters do not support a thesis.

upper.setting: Listen to an announcement in a university residence hall.
upper.script: Attention, residents of Wexford Hall. If you're returning in the autumn, you may store belongings in the basement over the summer, subject to a few conditions. Each resident is limited to four boxes and one large item, such as a bicycle or a suitcase. Everything must be labeled with your name and next year's room number, and nothing perishable or breakable will be accepted. Storage opens on the second of June, and the final drop-off is noon on the sixth. Anything left in rooms after that will be removed, and you'll be billed for its disposal. The hall can't accept responsibility for loss or damage, so take valuables home with you.

options: They will be moved to the basement for free.
They will be stored until the next term begins.
They will be given to other residents.
They will be removed at the owner's cost.
questions.why: 'Anything left in rooms after that will be removed, and you'll be billed for its disposal.'

questions.q: What does the speaker imply about valuable items?
options: They must be packed in a separate box.
The hall will not pay if they are lost.
They are kept in the hall office instead.
They count as one large item.
questions.why: 'The hall can't accept responsibility for loss or damage, so take valuables home with you.'

upper.subject: Economics
upper.script: Suppose I gave you the only telephone in the world. What would it be worth to you? Nothing, obviously. There'd be nobody to call. Give a second person a phone, and yours suddenly has some value. Add a million people, and it becomes something you can hardly live without. Economists call this a network effect: a product becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users grows. Notice how odd that is. With most goods, it makes no difference to me how many other people own one. My umbrella keeps me just as dry whether or not you have an umbrella too. Now, network effects have a couple of consequences worth remembering. First, getting started is brutally hard. Nobody wants to join an empty network, which is why new platforms so often give their service away for free at the beginning. They're buying a crowd. Second, once a network gets big enough, it tends to pull ahead and stay ahead. A competitor might offer something technically superior and still fail, because what people are really paying for isn't the technology. It's access to everyone else. So when you hear that a market has ended up with one giant firm, don't assume the best product won. Sometimes it's simply the one that got big first.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why some products gain value as more people use them
How the telephone was invented and sold
Why new companies should charge low prices
How governments control very large firms
questions.why: The professor defines a network effect, 'a product becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users grows', and gives two consequences.

questions.q: Why does the professor mention an umbrella?
options: To give an example of a product that people rarely share
To show that cheap goods lose value quickly
To contrast an ordinary good with a networked one
To explain why some products are sold in pairs
questions.why: 'With most goods, it makes no difference to me how many other people own one.' The umbrella is that ordinary case, unlike the telephone.

questions.q: According to the professor, why do new platforms often offer their service for free?
options: To test whether their technology works
To avoid paying taxes at the beginning
To prove that they are better than their larger rivals
To build up a large number of users quickly
questions.why: 'Nobody wants to join an empty network, which is why new platforms so often give their service away for free ... They're buying a crowd.'

questions.q: What does the professor imply about a market that is dominated by one giant firm?
options: The firm must have broken competition laws.
Its product may not be the best one available.
It will soon be replaced by a newer rival.
It probably offers its service free of charge.
questions.why: 'Don't assume the best product won. Sometimes it's simply the one that got big first.'

upper.subject: Literature
upper.script: The Iliad runs to more than fifteen thousand lines, and it took shape before the Greeks were widely using writing. So how on earth did anyone remember it? For a long time, the assumption was that poets simply had extraordinary memories and recited the poem word for word. Then, in the nineteen thirties, a young American scholar named Milman Parry tried something different. Instead of only studying old texts, he traveled to the Balkans, where singers still performed long heroic poems without being able to read, and he recorded them. What he found was that the singers weren't reciting from memory at all. They were composing as they sang. How? They'd absorbed a huge stock of ready-made phrases, each one shaped to fit the rhythm of a line. Think of Homer's 'swift-footed Achilles' or 'rosy-fingered dawn.' Readers today may find those repetitions tedious, but for the poet, they were building blocks. Whole scenes, like a feast, followed familiar patterns too. And here's the part I find most striking. The singers insisted that they sang a story exactly the same way every time. The recordings showed otherwise: no two performances matched. For them, 'the same' meant the same story, not the same words. So perhaps we should think of an epic less as a fixed text and more as a tradition of performances.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why the Iliad was finally written down
How modern readers should study Homer's language
How poets performed long poems without written texts
Why Balkan singers stopped performing heroic poems
questions.why: The professor asks how anyone remembered so long a poem and answers that singers composed as they sang, using ready-made phrases.

questions.q: What did Milman Parry do that earlier scholars had not done?
options: He translated the Iliad into a modern language.
He recorded living singers who could not read.
He counted the number of lines in the poem.
He taught Balkan singers to read old texts.
questions.why: 'Instead of only studying old texts, he traveled to the Balkans, where singers still performed ... without being able to read, and he recorded them.'

questions.q: Why does the professor mention "swift-footed Achilles"?
options: To show that Homer's heroes were skilled athletes
To point out a mistake in a modern translation
To explain why modern readers find the poem exciting
To illustrate the ready-made phrases poets relied on
questions.why: It is given as an example of the 'ready-made phrases, each one shaped to fit the rhythm of a line'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the singers Parry recorded?
options: They did not think of a poem as a fixed set of words.
They refused to let their performances be compared.
They had learned their poems from printed books.
They changed the story completely each time.
questions.why: They said they sang a story 'exactly the same way', yet no two performances matched: 'the same' meant 'the same story, not the same words'.

email.scenario: You are a student at a university. The final exam schedule was posted this morning, and you noticed that two of your exams, Introduction to Statistics and World History, are both scheduled for Thursday, December 17, at 9:00 a.m. You cannot be in two rooms at once. Your statistics instructor, Professor Whitfield, has told the class to contact her about any scheduling problems. You decide to write to her.
email.subject: Two final exams at the same time
bullets: Explain the problem with your exam schedule.
Suggest a way to solve the problem.
Ask what you need to do next.
email.model:
Dear Professor Whitfield,

I am a student in your Introduction to Statistics class, and I am writing because I have a problem with the final exam schedule that was posted this morning. Your exam is on Thursday, December 17, at 9:00 a.m., and my World History exam is at exactly the same time in a different building.

Since I cannot attend both, I would like to suggest taking the statistics exam at another time. I am free on Thursday afternoon and all day Friday, and I would be happy to take it with another section or in your office, whichever is easier for you.

Could you please let me know what I need to do next? If there is a form to complete or an office I should contact, I will do so right away. I can also send you a copy of my schedule.

Thank you very much for your help.

Sincerely,
Camila Duarte

professor.name: Dr. Navarro
professor.post: This week we are examining how technology shapes relationships. Billions of people now use social media to share news, photos, and opinions with friends and strangers. Some researchers argue that these platforms strengthen our ties by keeping us in touch across long distances. Others claim that time spent online replaces deeper, face-to-face contact and leaves people lonelier. What is your view? Has social media made people more connected or more isolated, and why?

students.name: Thabo
students.post: I believe social media has made us more connected. My family lives in three different countries, and before these apps existed we spoke only a few times a year. Now we share photos and messages every day in a group chat. I know what my cousins are doing, and I feel much closer to them than my parents did to their relatives.

students.name: Elif
students.post: In my opinion, people are more isolated now. We may have hundreds of online friends, but most of those relationships are shallow. I often see groups of friends sitting together in a café while each person looks at a phone. Liking someone's photo takes one second, and it is not the same as really listening to them.

discussion.model: I think social media can do both, but in my experience it has made people more connected overall. Thabo's example of a family spread across several countries is convincing, and I would add another kind of connection that he did not mention: people with unusual interests or problems can now find others like them. A teenager in a small town who loves astronomy, or someone learning a rare language, used to have no one to talk to. Today such people can join online communities and feel that they belong somewhere. I understand Elif's point that many online friendships are shallow, and it is true that phones sometimes interrupt real conversations. However, that is a problem of how we use the technology, not of the technology itself. If people set limits, for example by putting their phones away during meals, they can enjoy both kinds of contact.

repeat.scenario: You are learning how to volunteer at an animal shelter. Listen to your supervisor and repeat what he says. Repeat only once.

interview.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about shopping habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

questions.q: Thank you for joining me today. I'd like to begin with a recent experience. Please tell me about the last time you bought something that you were really pleased with. What was it, and why were you happy with it?
questions.model: A few weeks ago, I bought a secondhand bicycle, and I am still very pleased with it. I had been taking the bus to the university every day, which was slow and cost me quite a lot each month. I found the bike on a website where students sell things they no longer need, and the price was less than half of what a new one costs. The owner let me ride it around the block before I paid, so I knew that the brakes and the gears worked well. Now I get to class in fifteen minutes, I save money, and I get some exercise at the same time. It was easily my best purchase this year.

questions.q: Some people enjoy going to stores in person, while others would rather buy almost everything online. Which do you prefer, and why?
questions.model: I prefer shopping online for most things, mainly because it saves time. I have classes all day and a part-time job in the evening, so I can't easily get to the stores before they close. Online, I can compare prices from several sellers in a few minutes and read what other buyers thought of the product. That said, there are some things I always buy in person. Shoes are a good example, because sizes differ so much between brands, and I also like to choose my own fruit and vegetables. So I would say I do about three-quarters of my shopping online and the rest in real stores.

questions.q: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people believe that discounts and sales encourage shoppers to spend more money than they had planned. Do you agree or disagree? Why?
questions.model: Yes, I mostly agree. When people see a sign that says fifty percent off, they focus on how much they are saving rather than on how much they are spending. I have done this myself. Last winter I went into a store for a pair of gloves and came out with a jacket as well, only because it was on sale. I didn't really need it, and I have worn it twice. Sales also create a feeling of hurry, because the offer ends soon, so shoppers don't take time to think. Of course, a sale is useful if you were already planning to buy that item. The trick, I think, is to make a list first and keep to it.

questions.q: Here is my last question. Do you think schools should teach students how to manage their money, for example how to plan a budget and compare prices? Why or why not?
questions.model: Yes, I strongly believe schools should teach this. Managing money is a skill that everyone needs, but many young people only learn it by making expensive mistakes. When I first lived away from home, I spent most of my monthly budget in two weeks because nobody had shown me how to plan. A short course could cover simple things, such as writing a budget, comparing prices, and understanding how interest on a loan works. Some people argue that parents should teach these things, but not every parent has the time or the knowledge. If schools include this, every student gets the same chance to start adult life with good habits.
